title: [A2 • Band 4.0] Bài 312: The Singing Hominin: Roots of Melody
passageHtml:
PASSAGE 312 (LEVEL A2 • BAND 4.0)

The Singing Hominin: The Evolutionary Roots of Melody

Paragraph 1. For hundreds of years, many thinkers believed that music was just a fun hobby. They thought humans invented speech first and only added music much later. However, in 1871, scientist Charles Darwin had a different idea. He suggested that early humans sang musical sounds before they learned to talk with words. He thought early singing worked like the songs of birds to attract partners. Later in the twentieth century, some scientists still disagreed and said music did not help humans survive.

Paragraph 2. Today, researcher Dr. Steven Mithen shows that music is very important to human life. Every culture in the world has music, and human brains are built for it. Little babies understand musical tones and soft melodies months before they know the meaning of spoken words. Around the world, mothers naturally use gentle, sing-song voices to calm crying babies. Brain pictures also prove that listening to music wakes up deep parts of the brain linked to feelings and friendship.

Paragraph 3. Dr. Mithen thinks early human ancestors did not separate talking and singing. Instead, they used musical calls and hand movements together. These musical calls helped early groups work together during dangerous hunting trips, stop fights, and feel safe as a team. Much later, modern humans split these sounds into two paths. Speech became great for sharing facts, while music kept its power over human feelings. In this way, music acted like social glue that helped humans build big, friendly towns.
